questions.q: What are the three distinct time periods presented in the three stanzas of the poem "A Photograph"?
questions.a: The three time periods are: (1) the mother's childhood (the photograph scene), (2) the mother's adulthood when she looks at the photograph and laughs, and (3) the present where the poet reflects on her mother's death. A wrong answer (e.g., saying all stanzas are in the present) reveals the student hasn't grasped the temporal shifts that structure the narrative.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the poem's narrative structure differs from a linear story.
questions.a: The poem uses a non-linear structure: it begins with a past moment (the photograph), moves to an intermediate past (mother recalling it), and ends in the present (poet's grief). A linear story would tell events in chronological order. A wrong answer (e.g., "it goes in order") shows the student misses the deliberate time jumps that create emotional depth.

questions.q: Apply the concept of narrative arc (exposition, rising action, climax, resolution) to the poem. Which stanza serves as the climax and why?
questions.a: Stanza 2 is the climax: the mother's laughter at the photograph reveals her joy and the bittersweet awareness of time passing. The exposition is stanza 1 (the photo described), rising action is the mother's reaction, and resolution is stanza 3 (the poet's silence after her mother's death). A wrong answer (e.g., picking stanza 1) indicates the student cannot map narrative elements onto a poetic structure.

questions.q: Analyze how the shift from third-person description in stanza 1 to first-person reflection in stanza 3 affects the narrative perspective.
questions.a: Stanza 1 objectively describes the photograph (third-person), creating distance; stanza 3 shifts to the poet's personal grief (first-person), closing the emotional gap. This shift mirrors the movement from observed memory to lived loss. A wrong answer (e.g., "no change in perspective") shows the student overlooks the narrative voice as a structural device.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the poem's three-stanza structure effectively conveys the theme of transience. Justify your answer.
questions.a: Yes, the three stanzas enact transience: each stanza represents a phase that has vanished—the childhood moment, the mother's later life, and now the mother herself. The structure itself embodies the theme. A wrong answer (e.g., "structure doesn't matter") reveals the student doesn't connect form to meaning.

questions.q: Create a fourth stanza that could follow the poem, maintaining its narrative structure and tone, imagining the poet's future reflection.
questions.a: A good response would add a stanza in first person, perhaps showing the poet now older, looking at the same photograph, continuing the cycle of memory and loss. A poor answer (e.g., a happy ending unrelated to the poem's tone) shows the student hasn't internalized the narrative logic.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Plot and narrative structure in a poem refer to the sequence of events and the way the story is organized, including the exposition, rising action, climax, and resolution, often conveyed through stanzas and shifts in time or ______.

Fill in the blank: Start by asking the student: "Have you ever looked at an old family ______ and felt a rush of memories from different times?" Then guide them to read the poem aloud, noticing the three stanzas.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify the three temporal shifts in the poem, explain how each stanza contributes to the narrative arc, and articulate the effect of the non-linear structure on the theme of loss and memory.
